newsitem.title: BELGIUM: EU ministers seek to sort out Turkey muddle.
newsitem.headline: EU ministers seek to sort out Turkey muddle.

text.p: The European Union will try to hammer out a coherent policy on relations with Ankara on Sunday, following the blunt rejection of Turkey's EU membership hopes by a number of the bloc's leaders.

At a meeting in the Dutch town of Apeldoorn, starting on Saturday and otherwise likely to be dominated by worries over Albania, EU foreign ministers will try to assuage fears that they have turned their back on Turkey, risking an angry Islamic backlash.

Trigger for the discussion was a flurry of undiplomatic comments about Turkey's fitness to be in the European club emanating last week from a meeting of mainly Christian Democrat EU leaders in Brussels.
Among those present were Chancellor Helmut Kohl, Spanish Prime Minister Jose Maria Aznar and Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi, effectively making the statement seem like EU policy.

Speaking for the leaders, former Belgian Prime Minister Wilfried Martens said the message of the meeting had been: "Turkey is not a candidate to become a member of the European Union, short-term or long."
Others said Turkey's human-right record was ruling it out, while an unspoken element was the question of whether the EU wanted to bring in a large Moslem nation.
EU sources said the outburst was set off mainly by Turkey's threats to block NATO enlargement unless it is brought into the EU. Ankara, they said, had completely misjudged Europe's reaction.

But domestic politics also played into the move, in particular Kohl's need to respond to his countrymen's deep concern about record unemployment. Germany has the EU's largest number of Turkish workers.
Whatever the reason behind the move, a number of countries, notably France, have rushed to distance themselves from it.

"I think it is important for the stability of the Union, that is to say for the stability of the whole of Europe, that the Turks retain a European prospect, even if we know that membership would not be realistic in the short-term," French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier said.
Despite the presence of its prime minister, Jean-Luc Dehaene, at the Christian Democrats' meeting, Belgium also emphasised that Turkey could be an EU member if it met economic and political criteria.

The United States has also been horrified by the idea of Turkey having the European door shut in its face. It despatched special envoy Carey Cavanaugh to various European capitals to discuss the issue.
Turkey itself has reacted angrily. Its EU ambassador told a Turkish news agency his country would consider ditching its customs union with the EU if it were ruled out as an eventual member.
Aid to help Turkey adjust to the customs has been blocked by Greece, Ankara's longtome rival, and the European Parliament, which is angry about Turkey's human-rights record.

Diplomats said they expected the EU foreign ministers would make clear that the bloc did not want to exclude Turkey from EU membership over the long-haul, although there was no question of it becoming a member anytime soon.

They would also seek ways of lifting the blocks on Trukish funding and discuss how to meet Turkish demands that it be included with other, more immediate, applicant countries at the EU summit in Amsterdam in June.
